title: Review 76: Young people and work report
author: SMARTcurriculum Network
summary: Chris Jones of the SMARTcurriculum Network reads Alan Milburn's criticism of an exam-obsessed English system alongside YouGov polling of over 1,000 teachers and the near one million 16-24 year olds classed as NEET. The poll finds most teachers think students are less prepared for work than before, that the curriculum over-weights exams, and that 98% want mandatory careers advice. He argues the English model is excellent at sorting by standardised assessment but narrowly optimised, so transferable capability goes undeveloped because it is not measured. He sets out the case for and against intervention on NEET figures and settles on targeted, system-aligned action. He then reframes so-called soft skills as high-complexity competencies that need structured practice and assessment, and treats careers education as a structural lever rather than a late add-on. His conclusion, drawing on Singapore and Finland, is that without resolving the tension between selecting and preparing learners, reform will stay superficial.
points: Teacher polling and NEET figures point to a system that is highly effective at producing exam results but poorly aligned with the realities of work.
Skills such as communication, collaboration and adaptive problem-solving are high-complexity competencies, and calling them soft hides how much instruction they need.
Because these competencies are not formally assessed they are not systematically taught, which is the structural contradiction at the heart of the problem.
Careers education delivered late in Year 10 or 11 has limited effect; it must shape curriculum design with sustained employer engagement from the start.
Singapore and Finland show that coherence among curriculum, assessment and teacher development matters more than any single policy intervention.
quotes: It represents a convergence point—where political review, workforce data, and professional sentiment are beginning to align around a single, uncomfortable conclusion: the English education system is no longer coherently aligned with the realities it is meant to serve.
The English education model is highly efficient at what it was designed to do: differentiate attainment through standardised assessment.
The result is a cohort of students who can succeed within the parameters of the system but struggle to translate that success into the fluid, ambiguous environments of modern work.
The most robust position sits between the two extremes. The scale of the NEET cohort suggests that passive reliance on market correction is insufficient.
Framing these as “soft” diminishes their significance and, more importantly, their instructional complexity.
If careers education is treated as a late-stage intervention—a set of conversations or guidance sessions in Year 10 or 11—it will have limited impact.

If character, creativity, collaboration, communication, and problem-solving are not formally assessed, measured or validated, they will remain secondary, regardless of how often they are referenced in policy documents or inspection frameworks.
The lesson is not that England should replicate these models directly. It is that alignment matters more than individual policy interventions.
